title: Which MongoDB alternative fits you?
guideLabel: See the full list of picks

questions.q: How much of your app can you change?
questions.hint: This one answer removes most of the list.

options.label: Keep my MongoDB code as it is
options.why: you want an engine that accepts MongoDB commands

options.label: Keep JSON documents, new query language is fine
options.why: you keep your data shape and change your data access code

options.label: Change the data model
options.why: you can redesign how data is stored

options.label: Not sure yet
options.why: the post says to stay on MongoDB until you know your route

options.label: AWS runs it for me
options.why: you want a managed AWS service

options.label: Azure runs it for me
options.why: you want a managed Azure service

options.label: We run it on our own servers
options.why: Amazon DocumentDB and DynamoDB are AWS services

options.label: Joins, reports and SQL
options.why: you want joins and the SQL tools analysts know

options.label: Known key lookups at large scale
options.why: you fetch items by key and know your questions up front

options.label: Heavy writes across many servers
options.why: its storage engine suits write-heavy work

options.label: Flexible documents and changing queries
options.why: you want to keep working with documents

questions.q: How big is your largest document?

options.label: Under 400 KB
options.why: DynamoDB's 400 KB item limit is not a problem at this size

questions.q: Do other systems read your change feed?
questions.hint: In MongoDB this is change streams. Most options have their own feed, so MongoDB's does not come along.

options.label: Yes, and it must keep working
options.why: you need a change feed on the other side

options.label: Yes, and I need before and after images
options.why: MongoDB 6.0 can switch on pre- and post-images per collection

options.label: No, nothing reads it
options.why: FerretDB does not document change streams, so this gap would not hurt you

postgres.name: PostgreSQL with JSONB
postgres.summary: A relational database with a JSON column type, so you get SQL, joins and flexible documents in one system.
postgres.bestWhen: reports and joins matter more to you than a drop-in swap.
postgres.watchOut: any update locks the whole row, so large documents that change a lot are a poor fit, and your queries become SQL.

docdb.name: Amazon DocumentDB
docdb.summary: A managed AWS service that emulates the MongoDB APIs on its own engine.
docdb.bestWhen: you are on AWS and your app sticks to the supported features.
docdb.watchOut: it is not MongoDB: wildcard and hashed indexes are not supported, and change streams do not work on elastic clusters.

azure.name: Azure DocumentDB
azure.summary: A managed service on an MIT-licensed engine built on PostgreSQL, described by Microsoft as 99.03% MongoDB-compatible.
azure.bestWhen: you are on Azure or want an engine whose licence you can read in full.
azure.watchOut: the 99.03% counts operators only, and commands such as bulkWrite are not supported.

ferret.name: FerretDB
ferret.summary: A free Apache 2.0 proxy that turns MongoDB queries into SQL on PostgreSQL.
ferret.bestWhen: you want self-hosted and permissively licensed, and can live without a few commands.
ferret.watchOut: transaction commit and abort are not implemented yet, and change streams are not documented as supported.

couchbase.name: Couchbase
couchbase.summary: A JSON document database with its own SQL-like language, SQL++.
couchbase.bestWhen: you like the document model and do not mind a different query language.
couchbase.watchOut: you change drivers and rewrite queries, and Community Edition stops at five nodes and 4 cores per node.

dynamo.name: Amazon DynamoDB
dynamo.summary: A serverless AWS database where you fetch items by key.
dynamo.bestWhen: you know every question your app will ask and you are on AWS.
dynamo.watchOut: items stop at 400 KB, there are no joins, and Streams history is removed after 24 hours.

cassandra.name: Apache Cassandra
cassandra.summary: A free, open source distributed database where any copy of a partition can take a write.
cassandra.bestWhen: write volume is your problem and you have people to run clusters.
cassandra.watchOut: no joins or sub-queries in its query language, and single-table writes are eventually consistent.

mongodb.name: Stay on MongoDB
mongodb.summary: Staying put is a valid answer. MongoDB has cross-document transactions, sharding and change stream images.
mongodb.bestWhen: your app uses features the alternatives list as missing or limited, or you are not sure of your route yet.
mongodb.watchOut: the server licence is the SSPL, Atlas Dedicated clusters start at $56.94 a month, and unindexed $lookup joins can be slow on large collections.
